statement: In people dependent on opioids in supervised withdrawal, mostly in hospital or prison (6 randomized trials, 436 people, in a Cochrane review searched to December 2016), buprenorphine compared with a reducing course of methadone did not detectably change completion of withdrawal treatment: about 55 against 53 in 100 in the review's illustration (risk ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.20; 5 trials, 457 people), an interval that rules out large differences but not a gain of up to about 11 completions in 100 with buprenorphine or a loss of about 5. Time in treatment did not differ clearly (2 trials, 82 people, low certainty). Withdrawal severity and side effects could not be pooled: two trials found no difference in severity, two found differences on some days in opposite directions, and three reported no significant side effects with either medicine. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: Buprenorphine and a slowly reducing course of methadone helped about the same share of people finish withdrawal treatment, about 55 and 53 in 100. There were only six small trials, mostly in hospitals or a prison, and they could not show whether withdrawal felt different with one or the other.
population: People dependent on opioids in supervised withdrawal (four inpatient trials, one prison, one outpatient), in 6 randomized trials pooled in a Cochrane review
outcome: Completion of withdrawal treatment, with time in treatment, withdrawal severity and adverse effects reported alongside
magnitude: Completion RR 1.04 (0.91 to 1.20), 5 trials, 457 participants, GRADE moderate; illustrative 528 against 549 per 1000 (editors' arithmetic for the interval: about 5 fewer to 11 more per 100). Time in treatment MD 1.30 days (-8.11 to 10.72), 2 trials, 82 participants, low. Severity and adverse effects not pooled.

evidence.extracted: No meta-analysis of severity: Petitjean 2002 found no difference in total severity but higher scores on one day with buprenorphine and on two later days with methadone; Seifert 2002 found lower scores with buprenorphine on two assessment days; Bickel 1988 and Umbricht 2003 found no significant difference; two trials did not report severity. Three trials reported no significant adverse effects in either arm.

evidence.extracted: Four of the six trials were inpatient (one in an AIDS service with admission for acute illness), one in a prison healthcare centre, and only one outpatient.

risk_of_bias.note: Allocation unclear in five of six trials and unblinded subjective ratings in two, but completion is objective.

inconsistency.note: The review describes the completion results as reasonably consistent.

indirectness.note: Worded for supervised settings, mostly inpatient or prison.

imprecision.note: Fewer than 300 events; the interval allows up to about 11 more or 5 fewer completions per 100.

publication_bias.note: No method described; recorded as unknown.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; imprecision -1 gives moderate, as the review rated completion. 'Does not detectably change' is used because the interval excludes large differences in either direction; the statement gives the range it cannot exclude. Status replicated: five trials contributing in the same direction.
